messages.subject: how to output runtime error line numbers?
parts:
OK, so I've done the little dance to get line numbers
in and would appreciate both help and feedback at this
point. Here's what I did in words:

1. Added two static int variables to the namespace
for the model. One holds the beginning and one the end
line of the next statement to be executed. My first thought
was to make them member variables in the model class, but
that would prevent functions from updating them.

2. I code generated everywhere to update them. Basically,
the statement class in the AST now holds a start and end
line. (I could add column numbers or remove the last line.)
So now the model is peppered with assignments to these
statics. (I hope that doesn't slow things down.)

3. I added methods in the model to access them. I
made them members, but I should probably make them static.

Now what I can't figure out at least at first glance is where
the error messages are getting printed. I looked through
services/command.hpp, which is where I suspected it would be,
but can only find a hard-coded output to std::cout for the
Newton optimizer.

I also saw that the "infomrational message" is cut-and-pasted
in two places in the code. I'd like to try to get rid of this
duplication if possible. But what I really want to know is
where the print's happening so that I can add the line numbers.

Thanks.

- Bob

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] how to output runtime error line numbers?
parts:
The prints all come from exceptions.

model::transform_inits catches and throws errors messages
from exceptions thrown in io_writer, while model::log_prob
throws exceptions while validating transformed parameters.

Value problems (NaNs, infs, etc) are handled in
src/stan/mcmc/hmc/hamiltonians/base_hamiltonian.hpp
which catches exceptions thrown by stan::model::gradient.

Great. That has a handle on the model, so I am able to
do the right thing.

...
parameters {
real<lower=0,upper=1> y;
}
model {
if (y < 0.01)
(-y) ~ beta(1,1);
}

Running this generates this warning (note the first line!):

Warning from statement starting at line=15 and ending at line=16
Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
stan::prob::beta_log: Random variable is -0.00415357, but must be >= 0!
If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.

Line 15 is the (-y) ~ line. The earlier lines were to
test that code was being generated properly in functions.
The reason the statement ends on line 16 is that the iterator
is running past where it ends.

Speaking of which, do you (Michael) want to rewrite this
message to suggest people look at n_divergent? This is
the old message that tells them it's basically OK to
diverge.

I see this in the main.cpp from cmdstan:

int main(int argc, const char* argv[]) {
try {
return stan::services::command<stan_model>(argc,argv);
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
std::cerr << std::endl << "Exception: " << e.what() << std::endl;
std::cerr << "Diagnostic information: " << std::endl << boost::diagnostic_information(e) << std::endl;
return -1;
}
}

Does this catch ever get called? I don't remember seeing exceptions
with diagnostic information, but I don't even know what that
boost call does. I could wrap up stan::services::command
to catch and rethrow an exception that contains line
numbers (both programatically and in the what() return).

Also, where are errors printed for optimization?
I only see catches for the Newton case.

I want to do this all in such a way that it'll work for
CmdStan, RStan, and PyStan easily, so any comments would be
greatly appreciated.

- Bob

First, THANK YOU BOB!  This has been a missing feature which has bugged me for ages.  I even made a few attempts at it but could never penetrate the parser far enough to figure out how to do it.

Anyway, would it maybe make sense to have the generated model code catch all exceptions and then update the message by including line numbers?  That way we don't have to update all callers that catch exceptions, just the model code.  Alternatively, we could have it catch exceptions and then rethrow a special Stan model exception which included the original exception plus this added information.  Then the variables that hold the line number information don't have to be member variables and can just be locals which may be faster.

Cheers,
Marcus

I can swot up on it).

template <typename E>

const int begin_;
const int end_;

located_exception : std::exception {

const int begin_;

: e_(e), begin_(begin), end_(end) { }

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] how to output runtime error line numbers?
parts:
It should compile, but whether or not it gets caught depends
on how you right the catch block. In order to catch the
exception you have to specify an explicit type,

try {
} catch(std::exception& e) {
// use e
}

which would mean doing something like

try {
} catch(located_exception<type>& e) {
// use e
}

But why use CRTP here instead of having located_exception
derive from std::exception or std::runtime_exception? The
latter two are nice because they’ll get caught by catches
looking for them.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] how to output runtime error line numbers?
parts:
> On Mar 4, 2015, at 8:13 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> It should compile, but whether or not it gets caught depends
> on how you right the catch block. In order to catch the
> exception you have to specify an explicit type,
>
> try {
> } catch(std::exception& e) {
> // use e
> }
>
> which would mean doing something like
>
> try {
> } catch(located_exception<type>& e) {
> // use e
> }
>
> But why use CRTP here

So that I could catch the RT. That is, if I have
located_exception<out_of_range> and that uses the CRTP
to inherit from out_of_range, I should be able to catch
an out of range exception. Of course, I'd then need to
cast down to located_exception<out_of_range>, which is
super ugly, so it's probably not much use.

Right now, we just brute-force handle all types of
exceptions the same way. I guess we'll just have to
keep doing that going forward and I'll just just a single
located_exception with no templating and just have everything
be super generic with no way of finding the type of the
nested exception other than using run-time type info (RTTI).

- Bob
